fable.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French fable, from Latin fābula, from fārī (“to speak, say”) + -bula (“instrumental suffix”).
fable.g: A fictitious narrative intended to enforce some useful truth or precept, usually with animals, etc. as characters; an apologue. Prototypical

fabric.e: Borrowed from French fabrique, from Latin fabrica (“a workshop, art, trade, product of art, structure, fabric”), from faber (“artisan, workman”).

fabulous.e: From Late Middle English fabulous, fabulose, from Latin fābulōsus (“celebrated in fable”); Equivalent to fable + -ous.
fabulous.g: Of or relating to fable, myth or legend.

face.e: From Middle English face, from Old French face, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“form, appearance”). Old English ansīen (“face”), Middle English neb (“face, nose”) (from Old English nebb), Middle English ler, leor, leer (“face, cheek, countenance”) (from Old English hlēor), and non-native Middle English vis (“face, appearance, look”).
face.g: The front part of the head of a human or other animal, featuring the eyes, nose, and mouth, and the surrounding area.

fact.e: From Old French fact, from Latin factum (“an act, deed, feat, etc.”); also Medieval Latin for “state, condition, circumstance”; neuter of factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Old/Middle French later evolved it into faict and fait.
fact.g: Something actual as opposed to invented.

faction.e: Borrowed from Middle French faction, from Latin factiō (“a group of people acting together, a political faction”), noun of process from perfect passive participle factus, from faciō (“do, make”).
faction.g: A group of people, especially within a political organization, which expresses a shared belief or opinion different from people who are not
A form of literature, film etc., that treats real people or events as if they were fiction; a mix of fact and fiction.

fade.e: From Middle English fade, vad, vade (“faded, pale, withered, weak”), from Middle Dutch vade (“weak, faint, limp”), from Old French fade (“weak, witless”), of obscure origin. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fatidus, from Latin fatuus (“insipid”).
From Middle English fade, fede, of uncertain origin.

fail.e: From Middle English failen, borrowed from Old French falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallire, alteration of Latin fallere (“to deceive, disappoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰāl- (“to lie, deceive”) or Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”).

failure.e: From Anglo-Norman failer, from Old French faillir (“to fail”). Equivalent to fail + -ure.
failure.g: State or condition of not meeting a desirable or intended objective, opposite of success.

fain.e: From Middle English fain (“enjoyable, pleasing; fond of; glad, pleased; good, suitable; happy, joyful”), from Old English fægen (“happy, joyful, fain”), from Proto-West Germanic *fagan (“glad”), from Proto-Germanic *faganaz (“glad”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“joyful; pretty”).
fain.g: Often followed by of: glad, well-pleased.

fain.e: From Middle English fain (“eagerly, willingly; gladly, joyfully”), from fain (adjective): see etymology 1.
fain.g: Chiefly preceded or followed by would.

faint.e: From Middle English faynt, feynt (“weak; feeble”), from Old French faint, feint (“feigned; negligent; sluggish”), past participle of feindre, faindre (“to feign; sham; work negligently”).
faint.g: Lacking strength; weak; languid; inclined to lose consciousness

faint.e: From Middle English feynen, from the adjective (see above).
faint.g: To lose consciousness through a lack of oxygen or nutrients to the brain, usually as a result of suddenly reduced blood flow (may be caused

fainting.e: From Middle English feinting, equivalent to faint + -ing.
fainting.g: An act of collapsing into a state of temporary unconsciousness.

faintness.e: From Middle English faintnesse, feintnesse, equivalent to faint + -ness.
faintness.g: The property of being or feeling faint.

fair.e: From Middle English fayr, from Old English fæġer (“beautiful”), from Proto-West Germanic *fagr, from Proto-Germanic *fagraz (“appropriate, fitting, nice, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to attach, join; agreement, settlement”).
fair.g: Beautiful, of a pleasing appearance, with a pure and fresh quality.

fair.e: From Middle English feyre, from Old French foire, from Latin fēriae.
fair.g: A community gathering to celebrate and exhibit local achievements.

fairly.e: From Middle English fayrly, fayrely, vayrliche, equivalent to fair + -ly.
fairly.g: In a fair manner; fair; not biased or skewed or favouring a certain party.

fairness.e: From Middle English fairness, fæȝernesse, from Old English fæġernes (“fairness; beauty; pleasantness”), equivalent to fair + -ness.
fairness.g: The property of being fair or equitable.

faith.e: From Middle English faith (also fay), borrowed from Old French fei, feid, from Latin fidem. Old French had as a final devoiced allophone of /ð/ from lenited Latin /d/; this eventually fell silent in the 12th century. The -th of the Middle English forms is most straightforwardly accounted for as a direct borrowing of a French.
faith.g: A trust or confidence in the intentions or abilities of a person, object, or ideal from prior empirical evidence.

faithful.e: From Middle English feithful, equivalent to faith + -ful.
faithful.g: Loyal; adhering firmly to person or cause.

faithfully.e: From Middle English feithfulli, equivalent to faithful + -ly.

faithfulness.e: From Middle English feithfulnesse, equivalent to faithful + -ness.

faithless.e: From Middle English feithles, equivalent to faith + -less.
faithless.g: Lacking faith; lacking belief in something.

falcon.e: From Middle English faucoun, falcon, faulcon, from Old French falcun, from Late Latin falcō (“falcon”), of Germanic origin, probably via Frankish *falkō (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *falkô (“falcon”), from Proto-Indo-European *pol̑- (“pale”), from *pel- (“fallow”).
falcon.g: Any bird of the genus Falco, all of which are birds of prey.

fall.e: Verb from Middle English fallen, from Old English feallan (“to fall, fail, decay, die, attack”), from Proto-West Germanic *fallan (“to fall”), from Proto-Germanic *fallaną (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃elh₁- (“to collapse, fall; to destroy”). Noun from Middle English fal, fall, falle.
Perhaps from the north-eastern Scottish pronunciation of whale.
fall.g: The cry given when a whale is sighted, or harpooned.

fallen.g: Having dropped by the force of gravity.

fallow.e: From Middle English falwe, from Old English fealh, fealg (“fallow land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgu (compare Saterland Frisian Falge, West Frisian falig, felling, Dutch valg, German Felge), from Proto-Indo-European *polḱéh₂ (“arable land”) (compare Gaulish olca, Russian полоса́ (polosá)).
fallow.g: Ground ploughed and harrowed but left unseeded for one year.

fallow.e: From Middle English falowen, falwen, from Old English fealgian (“to fallow; break up land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgōn (“to fallow”).
fallow.g: To make land fallow for agricultural purposes.

false.e: From Middle English false, fals, from Old English fals (“false; counterfeit; fraudulent; wrong; mistaken”), from Latin falsus (“counterfeit, false; falsehood”), perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”). Reinforced in Middle English by Anglo-Norman and Old French fals, faus.

falsehood.e: From Middle English falshede, from false + -hede, equivalent to false + -hood.

falsely.e: From Middle English falsly, falsliche, equivalent to false + -ly.

falsify.e: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.
falsify.g: To alter so as to make false; especially when done with intent to deceive.

falter.e: From Middle English falteren (“to stagger; be unsteady, tremble, quiver; to stammer; be entangled, get caught”), further origin unknown. Probably from a North Germanic source such as Old Norse faltrask (“to hesitate, be puzzled, be encumbered”). May also be a frequentative of fold, although the change from d to t is unusual.

fame.e: From Middle English fame, from Old French fame (“celebrity, renown”), itself borrowed from Latin fāma (“talk, rumor, report, reputation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéh₂-meh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (“to speak, say, tell”).
fame.g: Something said or reported; gossip, rumour.

familiar.e: From Middle English familiar, familier, from Latin familiāris (“pertaining to servants; pertaining to the household”). By surface analysis, family + -ar. Piecewise doublet of familial.
familiar.g: Known to one, or generally known; commonplace.

family.e: From Late Middle English famylye, from Latin familia (“a household”).
family.g: A group of people who are closely related to one another (by blood, marriage or adoption); kin; in particular, a set of parents and their ch

famine.e: Borrowed from Middle French famine, itself from the root of Latin fames.
famine.g: Extreme shortage of food in a region.

famish.e: From Middle English famisshe, from famen (“starve”), from Old French afamer, ultimately from Latin famēs (“hunger”).
famish.g: To starve (to death); to kill or destroy with hunger.

famous.e: From Middle English famous, from Anglo-Norman famous, from Latin fāmōsus, equivalent to fame + -ous.

fan.e: From Middle English fan, inherited from Old English fann (“a winnowing, fan”), derived from Latin vannus (“fan for winnowing grain”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
fan.g: A hand-held device consisting of concertinaed material, or slats of material, gathered together at one end, that may be opened out into the

fan.e: Clipping of fanatic, originally in US baseball slang. Possibly influenced by fancy (“group of sport or hobby enthusiasts”), i.e. fancy boy (“fan”).
fan.g: A person who is fond of something or someone, especially an admirer of a performer or aficionado of a sport.

fang.e: From clipping of fangtooth, from Middle English *fangtooth, *fengtooth, from Old English fengtōþ (“molar tooth”), from feng, preterite of fōn (“to catch, take, seize”).
fang.g: A long, pointed canine tooth used for biting and tearing flesh.

fang.e: From Middle English fangen, fongen, from Old English fōn (“to take, grasp, seize, catch, capture, make prisoner, receive, accept, assume, undertake, meet with, encounter”), and Old Norse fanga (“to fetch, capture”), both from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną, *fangōną (“to catch, capture”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to attach”).

fantasy.e: Noun inherited from Middle English fantasie, from Old French fantasie (“fantasy”), from Latin phantasia (“imagination”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía, “apparition”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός (phantós, “visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to make visible”); from the same root as φάος (pháos, “light”).
fantasy.g: That which comes from one's imagination or the act of imagining things.

far.e: From Middle English ferre, fer, Old English feor, feorr, from Proto-Germanic *ferrai.

far.g: Emmer (a type of wheat), especially in the context of Roman use of it.

far-off.g: Distant or remote (in space, or less commonly in time).

faraway.g: Distant or remote in time or space.

fare.e: From Middle English fare, from a merger of Old English fær (“journey, road”) and faru (“journey, companions, baggage”), from Proto-Germanic *farą and *farō (“journey, fare”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“a going, passage”).
fare.g: A going; journey; travel; voyage; course; passage.

fare.e: From Middle English faren, from Old English faran (“to travel, journey”), from Proto-West Germanic *faran, from Proto-Germanic *faraną, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“a going, passage”).
fare.g: Used to express evaluations [with adverbial complement].

farewell.e: From Middle English farewel, from fare wel! (and the variants with the personal pronoun "fare ye well" and "fare you well" used in the Renaissance), an imperative expression, possibly further derived from Old English *far wel!, equivalent to fare (“to fare, travel, journey”) + well, said to somebody setting out on a journey.
farewell.g: A wish of happiness or safety at parting, especially a permanent departure.

farm.e: From Middle English ferme, farme (“rent, revenue, produce, factor, stewardship, meal, feast”), influenced by Anglo-Norman ferme (“rent, lease, farm”), from Medieval Latin ferma, firma. There is debate as to whether Medieval Latin acquired this term from Old English feorm (“rent, provision, supplies, feast”).
farm.g: A place where agricultural and similar activities take place, especially the growing of crops or the raising of livestock.

farm.e: From Middle English fermen, from Anglo-Norman fermer (“to let out for a fixed payment, lease, rent”) ultimately from the same Old English source as Etymology 1.
farm.g: To work on a farm, especially in the growing and harvesting of crops.

farmer.e: From Middle English fermour (“a steward, bailliff, collector of taxes”), from Old French fermier (“a farmer, a lessee, husbandman, bailliff”), from Medieval Latin firmarius (“one to whom land is rented, a collector of taxes, deputy”), from firma; equivalent to farm + -er.
farmer.g: Someone or something that farms, as:

farther.g: Alternative form of further. (See also the usage notes at further.)

farthing.e: From Middle English ferthing, from Old English fēorþing, fēorþung (“a quarter, fourth part, farthing”), from fēorþa (“fourth”), from Proto-Germanic *fedurþungaz (“a quarter”), probably influenced by Old Norse fjórðungr (“a fourth part, quarter”). Equivalent to fourth + -ing; compare English riding (“third part”).
farthing.g: A quarter of any monetary unit or measure.

fashion.e: From Middle English facioun, from Anglo-Norman fechoun (compare Jersey Norman faichon), variant of Old French faceon, fazon, façon (“fashion, form, make, outward appearance”), from Latin factiō (“a making”), from faciō (“do, make”); see fact.
fashion.g: A current (constantly changing) trend, favored for frivolous rather than practical, logical, or intellectual reasons.

fast.e: From Middle English fast, fest, from Old English fæst (“firm, secure”), from Proto-West Germanic *fast, from Proto-Germanic *fastuz; see it for cognates and further etymology. The development of “rapid” from an original sense of “secure” apparently happened first in the adverb and then transferred to the adjective.
fast.g: Firmly or securely fixed in place; stable.

fast.e: From Middle English fast, faste, from Old English fæste, from fæst + -e (adverb-forming suffix).
fast.g: In a firm or secure manner, securely; in such a way as not to be moved; safe, sound .

fasten.e: From Middle English fastenen, from Old English fæstnian, from Proto-West Germanic *fastinōn (“to secure, fasten”). Equivalent to fast + -en.
fasten.g: To attach or connect in a secure manner.

fasting.g: Abstinence or mortification for religious reasons, especially abstinence from food.

fat.e: From Middle English fat, from Old English fǣtt (“fatted, fat”), from Proto-West Germanic *faitid (“fatted”), originally the past participle of the verb *faitijan (“to make fat”), from *fait (“fat”).
fat.g: Carrying more fat than usual on one's body; plump; not lean or thin.

fat.e: From Middle English fat, fatt, fatte, from the adjective above, and possibly from Old English fǣt (“fat”, recorded once), from Proto-West Germanic *fait, from Proto-Germanic *faitą, *faitaz (“fat”).
fat.g: A specialized animal tissue with high lipid content, used for long-term storage of energy: fat tissue.

fatal.e: From Middle French fatal, from Latin fātālis (“fatal”).
fatal.g: Proceeding from, or appointed by, fate or destiny.

fate.e: From Middle English fate, from Latin fāta (“prediction”), plural of fātum, from fātus (“spoken”), from for (“to speak”). In this sense, displaced native Old English wyrd, whence Modern English weird.
fate.g: The presumed cause, force, principle, or divine will that predetermines events.

father.e: From Middle English fader, from Old English fæder, from Proto-West Germanic *fader, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr, possibly from *peh₂- + *-tḗr.
father.g: A male parent, especially of a human; a male who parents a child (which he has sired, adopted, fostered, etc.).

father-in-law.e: From Middle English fader in lawe, fadyr-in-lay, fader yn lawe, equivalent to father + -in-law.

fatherless.e: From Middle English faderles, federles, from Old English fæderlēas, from Proto-Germanic *fadērlausaz, equivalent to father + -less.

fathom.e: From Middle English fathome, fadom, fadme (“unit of length of about six feet; depth of six feet for nautical soundings; (loosely) cubit; ell”), from Old English fæþm, fæþme (“encircling or outstretched arms, bosom, embrace; envelopment; control, grasp, power; fathom (unit of measurement); cubit”), from Proto-West Germanic *faþm (“outstretched arms, embrace.
fathom.g: A man's armspan, generally reckoned to be six feet (about 1.8 metres). Later used to measure the depth of water, but now generally replaced

fatling.g: A young animal (especially a calf or lamb) which has been fattened for slaughter.

fatness.e: From Middle English fatnesse, fattenesse, from Old English fǣtnes (“fatness, the richest part of anything”), equivalent to fat + -ness.
fatness.g: The state, quality, or condition of being fat.

fault.e: From Middle English faute, faulte, from Anglo-Norman faute, Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita (“shortcoming”), feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”).
fault.g: Culpability; the responsibility for a blameworthy event.

favor.e: From Middle English favour, favor, faver, from Anglo-Norman favour, from mainland Old French favor, from Latin favor (“good will; kindness; partiality”), from faveō (“to be kind to”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂weh₁yeti (“to be favourable to”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine, glow light”).
favor.g: A kind or helpful deed; an instance of voluntarily assisting (someone).

favorable.e: From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favor + -able.

favourable.e: From Middle English favourable, from Old French favorable, from Latin favōrābilis, from favor. By surface analysis, favour + -able.

fawn.e: From Middle English fawne, fowne, foun, from Old French faon, foon, feon, from Vulgar Latin *fētōnem, from Latin fētus (“offspring, young”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle, nurse”).
From Middle English fawnen, from Old English fagnian, alternative form of fæġnian (“to celebrate”), whence Middle English fainen, English fain.
fawn.g: To show devotion or submissiveness by wagging its tail, nuzzling, licking, etc.
